newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian stocks slide to slow, but no quick fix seen.
newsitem.headline: Indian stocks slide to slow, but no quick fix seen.

text.p: Reeling Indian stock markets may pause for a breather this week but a turnaround appears unlikely as investors continue to shy away, analysts and brokers said.
They said the outlook was marred by gloomy prospects for corporate profits. Many companies, hit by slowing demand and rising costs, delivered dismal first-half results.
The benchmark Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index of top-30 shares last week fell to a three-year low of 2,713.12 at one stage, before staging a technical rebound.
The index, which has fallen about 33 percent from its peak in June, ended the week down a hefty 64.30 points, or 2.22 percent over last week, at 2,826.20.
The fall for the third straight week, however, has made several stocks attractive. But buyers remained cautious because they were unsure the market had bottomed, the analysts said.
"The valuations are just unbelievable," said Bimal Parekh at BSE broking firm Jasvantlal Chhotalal & Co. "But people are not putting their money in."
He expects the market to be "absolutely lacklustre" in range-bound trade in the week ahead.
Some traders believe the fall in world share prices, especially in the United States, would channel more funds to emerging markets like India.
"We could see a sustained spell of profit-taking on the NYSE (New York Stock Exchange) in December 1996," Nucleus Securities Ltd said in a report published on Saturday.
"We remain optimistic to the potential of re-allocation of funds to under-performing markets like India in late December 1996 and early January 1997," the investment firm said.
"We also expect Japanese funds to take a closer look at the Indian market in 1997," it said.

Nucleus Securities forecast the BSE index to stay at the 2,800-2,975 range this week, supported by "well-entrenched" foreign funds which it said would step up buying ahead of the entry of newer funds early next year.
"A world stocks sell-off will depress domestic markets," said Chhotalal's Parekh. "The initial reaction will be down, down, down."

He said foreign funds, which had suffered heavy losses this year, would be reluctant to pump fresh funds into the country. Jatin Dedhia, a dealer at broker Russi Khambatta, said foreign funds were unlikely to buy Indian stocks until they were assured the market had bottomed out.
"At the moment, we see the (BSE) index losing another 100-odd points," he said.
